name: LuaJIT
baseline: Lua 5.4.7 (PUC-Rio reference interpreter, per the README environment table)
workload: kostya/benchmarks: Brainfuck interpreter (bench.b and mandel.b programs) and the primes test (Atkin sieve plus Trie prefix search), run as plain scripts under each interpreter.
claimed_speedup: bench.b: Lua/luajit 5.686 s vs Lua 37.051 s (about 6.5x, derived from page data). Primes: Lua/luajit 0.309 s vs Lua 1.056 s (about 3.4x, derived from page data). mandel.b: Lua/luajit 31.804 s (no plain-Lua row in the table).
compiler_and_flags: Interpreters run as `luajit file.lua` and `lua file.lua`; LuaJIT 2.1.1748495995 built with plain `make` from the openresty/luajit2 fork (docker/Dockerfile); README lists Lua 5.4.7 as the baseline.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Docker (Debian forky/sid) per README Environment section; base image and interpreter builds in docker/Dockerfile
stars_or_usage: 5.8k stars (repository description: mirror of the LuaJIT git repository)
tradeoffs: Lua 5.1-based, so Lua 5.3/5.4-only features (native integers and similar) are not available. JIT compilation is unavailable on some locked-down platforms. Memory use is higher on allocation-heavy tests (307.5 MB vs 145.2 MB for binarytrees in kostya/jit-benchmarks, 2023).
caveats: The benchmarked LuaJIT binary was built from the openresty/luajit2 fork, not from LuaJIT/LuaJIT directly. The README says the baseline is Lua 5.4.7 but docker/Dockerfile installs the Debian lua5.5 package (README and Dockerfile disagree, so the exact baseline version is uncertain). Numbers are derived ratios from single median timings on one Xeon box. Independent corroboration with the same direction: kostya/jit-benchmarks (2023, Ryzen 7 3800X) shows nbody 1.44 s vs 19.69 s and mandelbrot 0.5 s vs 5.39 s for Lua JIT vs Lua.
found_via: WebSearch 'interpreter benchmark comparison CPython Lua Ruby JavaScript engines results' -> github.com/kostya/jit-benchmarks; then kostya/benchmarks README (UPDATE: 2026-07-19) opened and the Dockerfile read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: PyPy
workload: kostya/benchmarks (Brainfuck bench.b, matmul, primes, JSON, base64) and attractivechaos/plb2 (nqueen, matmul, sudoku, bedcov), same Python source run under CPython and PyPy.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks: bench.b 9.398 s vs CPython 61.009 s (about 6.5x, derived from page data); matmul 3.263 s vs 136.267 s (about 42x, derived); primes 0.617 s vs 1.725 s (about 2.8x, derived); JSON 0.606 s vs 0.936 s (about 1.5x, derived). base64 is slower: 3.534 s vs 3.099 s. plb2 (M1): nqueen 6.91 s vs 159.97 s, matmul 4.89 s vs 117.81 s, sudoku 8.82 s vs 52.88 s, bedcov 6.27 s vs 42.84 s.
compiler_and_flags: PyPy 7.3.23 (Python 3.11.15 compatible) release tarball run as `pypy file.py` vs CPython 3.14.6 (docker/Dockerfile); plb2 used PyPy 7.3.14 vs CPython 3.11.7.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Docker (Debian forky/sid) per README Environment section; base image and interpreter builds in docker/Dockerfile; plb2 numbers on Apple M1 MacBook Pro
tradeoffs: Drop-in CPython alternative but lags CPython versions (3.11 compatible here vs 3.14), C extensions go through a slower cpyext layer, warm-up is needed and memory use is higher (bench.b: 60.19 + 30.10 MiB vs 11.38 + 0.00 MiB for CPython in the kostya tables); a 2018 hello-world startup test (bdrung/startup-time, Intel i5-2400S) put PyPy 5.8.0 at 27.53 ms vs 25.84 ms for CPython 3.6.3.
caveats: PyPy is slower than CPython on the kostya base64 test (3.534 s vs 3.099 s), so the win is workload dependent. CPython baseline in kostya is the stock interpreter without its experimental JIT. Ratios are derived from medians on one machine.
found_via: kostya/benchmarks README (opened) and attractivechaos/plb2 README (opened), surfaced by WebSearch 'Python implementation faster than CPython benchmark pyperformance speedup github'

name: TruffleRuby
workload: kostya/benchmarks: Brainfuck bench.b, matmul, primes, JSON, base64, run as the same Ruby scripts under each Ruby implementation.
claimed_speedup: bench.b: Ruby/truffleruby 5.169 s vs Ruby 74.107 s (about 14x, derived from page data) and vs Ruby --jit 30.807 s. matmul: 17.776 s vs Ruby 211.868 s (about 12x, derived) and vs Ruby --jit 152.991 s. primes: 0.871 s vs Ruby 1.794 s and Ruby --jit 1.118 s. Slower cases in the same tables: JSON 11.341 s vs Ruby 1.031 s, base64 8.789 s vs Ruby 1.861 s. The README itself says TruffleRuby is 'by far the fastest Ruby implementation on the yjit-bench benchmark suite' (its linked blog post was not opened).
compiler_and_flags: TruffleRuby 34.0.1 native and JVM release tarballs vs CRuby 4.0.6 built with CC=clang ./configure --enable-yjit (docker/Dockerfile); scripts run via `truffleruby`, `ruby`, `ruby --jit`.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Docker (Debian forky/sid) per README Environment section; base image and interpreter builds in docker/Dockerfile
tradeoffs: Needs warm-up and much more memory (bench.b: 197.19 + 693.00 MiB vs 12.12 + 0.00 MiB for CRuby in the kostya tables). README offers two configurations: Native (faster startup) and JVM (better peak performance).
caveats: TruffleRuby is slower than CRuby on the JSON (11x) and base64 (4.7x) tests in the same suite, so the speedup is workload dependent. Ratios are derived from single medians on one Xeon box. An older academic corroboration exists: smarr/are-we-fast-yet docs/performance.md (2016, JRuby+Truffle, TruffleRuby's predecessor) lists geomean 2.36x Java vs MRI 45.62x Java.
found_via: kostya/benchmarks README (opened); LangArena README and plb2 README list TruffleRuby as the Ruby contender

name: Codon
workload: attractivechaos/plb2: nqueen (15 queens), matmul (1500x1500) and sudoku (4000 puzzles); the same src/python/*.py files are run by CPython and compiled by `codon build -release -exe`.
claimed_speedup: codon* nqueen 2.82 s vs py:cpy 159.97 s (about 57x, derived from page data); matmul 2.49 s vs 117.81 s (about 47x, derived); sudoku 3.08 s vs 52.88 s (about 17x, derived). README: 'Typical speedups over vanilla Python are on the order of 10-100x or more, on a single thread'; fib(40) 17.979 s in python3 vs 0.276 s with codon run -release.
compiler_and_flags: Codon 0.18.0, `codon build -release -exe` (plb2 src/python/Makefile); CPython 3.11.7 run directly.
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Pro (plb2 README; hyperfine timing)
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler for Python-syntax programs, not a drop-in CPython replacement; compile step adds seconds (4.28-6.42 s per program in kostya/jit-benchmarks).
caveats: plb2's Codon row is not plotted in the figure (Plot = N) but is listed in the table. The numbers are Codon 0.18.0 on Apple M1 (plb2 commit 'updated Codon to v0.18.0', 2025-01-30). In kostya/jit-benchmarks (2023) Codon produced no result for pidigits and regexdna, which hints at compatibility limits. The README's own fib and pi numbers state no hardware.
found_via: attractivechaos/plb2 README (opened) surfaced by WebSearch 'interpreter benchmark comparison ...'; cross-checked with exaloop/codon README

name: GraalPy
workload: attractivechaos/plb2: nqueen, matmul, sudoku, bedcov in plain Python; README separately cites the Python Performance Benchmark Suite.
claimed_speedup: plb2 py:graal+ (Graal EE 23.1.1) vs py:cpy: nqueen 4.38 s vs 159.97 s (about 37x, derived from page data); matmul 16.22 s vs 117.81 s (about 7x, derived); bedcov 12.32 s vs 42.84 s (about 3.5x, derived); sudoku 59.52 s vs 52.88 s (slower). README: 'GraalPy is geomean ~4x faster than CPython on the official Python Performance Benchmark Suite'.
compiler_and_flags: Graal EE 23.1.1 (Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition) running the Python sources; CPython 3.11.7; no JVM flags stated.
tradeoffs: Runs on the JVM and needs JIT warm-up; README describes native extension module support as experimental.
caveats: plb2 measured the Enterprise Edition build, not the open source Community Edition that this repository produces, so the plb2 numbers may not carry over. GraalPy was slower than CPython on sudoku in the same table. The README's 4x geomean is a first-party claim whose pyperformance page was not opened. Python 3.13-compliant per README, older than the CPython in newer benchmarks.
found_via: attractivechaos/plb2 README (opened) py:graal+ row; WebSearch 'Python implementation faster than CPython ...' listed GraalPy

name: Cython
baseline: CPython 3 (kostya/jit-benchmarks 'Python3' rows; interpreter version not stated in the README)
workload: kostya/jit-benchmarks: benchmarks-game programs (binarytrees, fannkuchredux, mandelbrot, nbody, matmul and others) run as CPython scripts and as Cython-compiled .pyx files.
claimed_speedup: Cython vs Python3 best times: binarytrees 0.81 s vs 73.15 s; fannkuchredux 0.13 s vs 4.04 s; mandelbrot 0.43 s vs 37.52 s; nbody 0.56 s vs 53.72 s; matmul 0.39 s vs 22.73 s. Not faster on fasta-style text tests: knucleotide 8.33 s vs 8.41 s, regexdna 6.1 s vs 5.2 s.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README; Cython sources are in per-benchmark test.pyx files and use cdef static typing.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80 GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10 (README, round 1 dated 2023-02-28)
stars_or_usage: 10.9k stars; README cites more than 70 million PyPI downloads per month
tradeoffs: Needs a build step and a C/C++ compiler; the large speedups require cdef type annotations and C-level constructs, i.e. effectively a different (typed) program. Output can be C++ and linked from C++ code.
caveats: The nbody .pyx in the suite uses cdef structs, extern math.h and typed loops (Cythonized by Robert Bradshaw), so the numbers measure typed Cython, not unmodified Python. Cython compile time of 0.8-2.6 s per benchmark is excluded from the best-time column. The 2023 suite is old; the shootout was not rerun since round 1. Cython's README makes no numeric claim.
found_via: WebSearch 'interpreter benchmark comparison CPython Lua Ruby JavaScript engines results' -> github.com/kostya/jit-benchmarks (README opened; nbody/test.pyx read via raw.githubusercontent.com)

name: Spinel
workload: 28 benchmarks in the repository's benchmark/ directory (mandelbrot, fib, matmul, nqueens, sieve, binary_trees, json_parse, ao_render and others), compiled ahead of time to native executables by Spinel versus the same scripts run by CRuby.
claimed_speedup: 'Geometric mean: ~8.5x faster than Ruby 4.0.4 with --yjit across the 28 benchmarks (~15.2x against the interpreter)'. Examples vs YJIT: mandelbrot 18 ms vs 938 ms (53.6x), matmul 6.1 ms vs 201 ms (32.9x), binary_trees 2.7 ms vs 13 ms (4.7x), json_parse 28 ms vs 133 ms (4.7x), csv_process 95 ms vs 396 ms (4.2x).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3 builds the generated C; CRuby 4.0.4 (revision b89eb1bc) run with --disable-gems, and with --yjit for the JIT column; each cell is the mean of five runs under `perf stat -r 5`.
tradeoffs: An ahead-of-time compiler for a Ruby subset (see the README Supported Ruby Features section), not a drop-in interpreter: it does whole-program type inference, emits C and invokes the system cc. Compiled binaries start in about 0.8 ms.
caveats: First-party numbers with only a core count for hardware. Sub-10 ms cells are dominated by process startup (README says the ratios are lower bounds). The README itself warns the fib row (44.6x vs YJIT) reflects the C compiler folding a pure call tree at build time. The README also notes YJIT is essentially identical to the interpreter on mandelbrot, nqueens, matmul, partial_sums and sieve.
found_via: kostya/LangArena README (opened) lists Spinel as a Ruby contender; github.com/matz/spinel README and benchmark section opened

name: Wren
workload: Four micro/macro benchmarks from the repository's test/benchmark directory: method call, DeltaBlue, binary trees, recursive Fibonacci; best of ten runs, interpreter startup excluded.
claimed_speedup: Method call: wren 0.12 s vs lua 0.35 s, ruby 0.20 s, python3 0.78 s. Binary trees: wren 0.22 s vs lua 0.52 s, python3 0.38 s (luajit -joff 0.11 s and ruby 0.24 s). Recursive Fibonacci: wren 0.20 s vs lua 0.28 s, ruby 0.22 s, python3 0.57 s. DeltaBlue: wren 0.13 s vs python3 0.48 s.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; LuaJIT 2.0.2 run with the JIT disabled (-joff).
hardware: MacBook Pro 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7, 16 GB DDR3 (author's laptop)
tradeoffs: A different language (class-based, fibers, small standard library), not a Lua replacement; embeddable single-pass bytecode VM under 4,000 lines, compiles as C99 or C++98 and later. LuaJIT with the JIT enabled is faster, as the page itself admits.
caveats: Old first-party numbers measured against Lua 5.2.3, Python 2.7/3.3 and Ruby 2.0 on a 2014-era laptop with no compiler flags stated; modern Lua 5.4, CPython 3.12+ and Ruby 3.x are faster. Last commit is only a CI file edit. Wren is slower than LuaJIT with the JIT disabled on binary trees and recursive Fibonacci (the tests where LuaJIT was measured besides method call).
found_via: WebSearch 'interpreter benchmark comparison CPython Lua Ruby JavaScript engines results' listed wren.io/performance.html; the same page's source (doc/site/performance.markdown) opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: LuaJIT Remake
baseline: PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter (also compared with LuaJIT's interpreter)
workload: The repository's luabench suite (a variety of Lua benchmarks, geometric mean over all benchmarks, each repeated 5 times), interpreter tier only with GC turned off for all implementations.
claimed_speedup: 'our interpreter is 34.6% faster than LuaJIT's interpreter, and 185% faster than the official PUC Lua5.1 interpreter'
compiler_and_flags: Built with `python3 ljr-build make release` inside docker (compiler and flags not stated in the README); the PUC Lua and LuaJIT comparison builds are not described.
tradeoffs: Interpreter (and planned JIT tiers) are generated automatically from semantic bytecode descriptions; Lua 5.1 interpreter with a re-engineered runtime (tables use hidden classes). x86-64 Linux only.
caveats: Project is unfinished: garbage collection is not implemented (the README says GC was switched off for the competing implementations too), the package library and other standard-library functions are missing, and the multi-tier JIT is not complete, so the numbers are not production-comparable. Interpreter-only comparison, not against LuaJIT with JIT enabled. First-party numbers; the figure is an image and only the headline ratios appear in text. Last commit is 2025-02-18.
found_via: WebSearch 'Luau vs Lua 5.4 vs LuaJIT benchmark results github interpreter speed' -> sillycross.github.io 'Building the fastest Lua interpreter.. automatically!' (blocked); repo README opened

name: LuaAOT (lua-aot-5.4)
baseline: Lua 5.4.3 interpreter (the stock interpreter the fork is based on)
workload: Numerical Lua benchmarks (the repository's experiments directory, e.g. binarytrees.lua) compiled ahead of time to C with the luaot compiler, versus the regular Lua interpreter.
claimed_speedup: 'For numerical benchmarks it can be twice as fast as regular Lua. But overall, it is not as fast as LuaJIT or Pallene.'
compiler_and_flags: Generated C compiled with gcc -shared -fPIC -O2 (README usage example); no benchmark flags stated.
tradeoffs: Modified Lua 5.4.3 with an extra luaot compiler that translates Lua bytecode to C (jumps become gotos, no bytecode dispatch); keeps full Lua 5.4 semantics and is embeddable from C/C++, but compiled modules must be built per script.
caveats: The README gives only a qualitative '2x on numerical benchmarks' figure with no table, hardware or timings; the paper that holds the experiments is referenced but not named or opened (scripts and programs are in the experiments directory). Based on Lua 5.4.3 (older than 5.4.7/5.5). Gains vary by program.
found_via: WebSearch 'Luau "Lua 5.4" faster interpreter benchmark numbers' -> hugomg/lua-aot-5.4; README and repo page opened

name: Luau
baseline: Lua 5.x (PUC-Rio interpreter; the Luau docs compare with Lua 5.4)
workload: Interpreter dispatch speed (bytecode design and VM loop); the claim comes from the Luau performance page, which could not be opened.
claimed_speedup: No numbers recorded. Search snippet of luau.org/performance: the interpreter is 'noticeably faster than Lua 5.x (including Lua 5.4)' and 'pretty much as fast as LuaJIT 2.1 in interpreter mode'.
tradeoffs: Gradually typed language derived from Lua that keeps backward compatibility with Lua 5.1 (README); includes a type checker and, per the repository layout, a CodeGen directory for native code generation.
caveats: Tier D: luau.org/performance and the Luau docs repository were EGRESS_BLOCKED or 404, so the claim is from a search snippet only. The repository's bench/ directory contains a Python harness (bench.py, with a --vm option to compare VMs) but no stored Lua-vs-Luau results; running it against PUC Lua would give A-tier evidence. A search-result summary (not opened) also says Luau with partial native compilation is about 1.6x slower than LuaJIT 2.1 in JIT mode.
found_via: WebSearch 'Luau vs Lua 5.4 vs LuaJIT benchmark results github interpreter speed'; github.com/luau-lang/luau page and bench/ directory opened

name: QuickJS (quickjs-ng)
workload: Process start plus `console.log(1)` for each runtime, measured with the shell `time` builtin (txiki.js issue #301).
claimed_speedup: `./qjs -e "console.log(1)"` 0.005 s total vs `node -e "console.log(1)"` 0.054 s total (about 11x less startup time, derived from page data); txiki.js 0.115 s.
tradeoffs: Small embeddable engine that aims to support the latest ECMAScript specification; a bytecode interpreter without JIT (plb2 classes QuickJS as purely interpreted), used as the engine of runtimes such as txiki.js (the issue's own subject). Embeds from C and C++.
caveats: Startup only: sustained throughput is far worse than V8. In attractivechaos/plb2 (Apple M1) QuickJS 23-12-09 took nqueen 59.04 s and matmul 135.66 s vs Node 21.5.0 at 3.73 s and 2.88 s. The issue page states no software versions, hardware, OS or flags, and it is unclear whether its `qjs` was Bellard's original or the quickjs-ng fork (the entry's repository is the maintained fork).
found_via: WebSearch 'QuickJS vs Node.js V8 startup time benchmark ...' -> txiki.js issue #301 (opened); plb2 README (opened) for the throughput caveat

name: Shed Skin
workload: README: more than 80 non-trivial example programs (over 25,000 lines) from the repository's examples directory, plus the 'sieve' example with n=100000000.
claimed_speedup: 'a typical speedup of 1-100 times over CPython 3.14 (average 20 times, median 12 times)'. Sieve (n=100000000): cpython 3.10.6 13.4 s, cpython 3.11.0 11.4 s, nuitka 0.6.16 11.4 s, pypy 3.9.12 5.8 s, numba 0.56.4 2.5 s, shedskin 0.9.9 1.9 s (--int32).
compiler_and_flags: Generated C++ built with the system compiler (flags not stated in the README); shedskin 0.9.9 options --int32 --nowrap --nobounds in the fastest sieve row.
license: GPL-3.0-only (compiler) AND MIT (C++ runtime library, with BSD-3-Clause and BSL-1.0 parts)
tradeoffs: Only a restricted, implicitly statically typed subset of Python 3 compiles: about 25 stdlib modules, no external libraries, no nested functions or variable argument lists; programs often need refactoring. Output is standalone C++ or a Python extension module, so it can be linked from C++ code.
caveats: First-party README numbers with no hardware, no flags and no per-program table in text (the speedup chart is an image; the project's asv benchmark page lives on shedskin.github.io, which is blocked here and was not opened). The sieve table mixes CPython 3.10.6 and 3.11.0, and the README notes Numba defaults to int64 and would otherwise be just as fast, so the margin over Numba comes partly from the narrower int32 type. PyPy comparison figure is against CPython 3.10.
found_via: WebSearch 'Python implementation faster than CPython benchmark pyperformance speedup github C++ interpreter'; README raw and repo page opened

name: Pyston
language: C (CPython 3.8.12 fork with a DynASM JIT)
workload: Web-serving macrobenchmarks (the pyston/macrobenchmarks repository is a submodule).
claimed_speedup: 'Pyston full ... is roughly 30% faster than CPython on web serving macrobenchmarks'; 'Pyston lite ... is roughly 10% faster on macrobenchmarks'.
tradeoffs: Pyston-full is API compatible but not ABI compatible with CPython (extensions need recompiling); Pyston-lite is a pip-installable JIT extension for Python 3.7-3.10 only. Targets old Python versions and is no longer maintained.
caveats: The repository header says 'No longer maintained'; last commit 2024-08-12. The baseline is CPython 3.8.12, far older than current CPython. README gives no hardware, flags or per-benchmark numbers. License is the CPython/PSF license file; DynASM, LuaJIT and LLVM pieces carry their own licenses.
found_via: WebSearch 'Python implementation faster than CPython benchmark ...' listed Pyston; repo page and README opened

name: Bun
language: Rust/TypeScript with the C++ JavaScriptCore engine (repository page language list)
workload: attractivechaos/plb2: nqueen (15 queens), matmul (1500x1500), sudoku (4000 puzzles), bedcov (1M intervals) in plain JavaScript, Bun vs Node with JIT enabled.
claimed_speedup: js:bun+ (Bun 1.0.20) vs js:node+ (Node 21.5.0): nqueen 3.11 s vs 3.73 s; matmul 1.75 s vs 2.88 s (about 1.6x, derived from page data); sudoku 3.07 s vs 3.77 s; bedcov 2.32 s vs 2.45 s. The README text says Bun and Node 'perform well' and are about twice as fast as PyPy.
compiler_and_flags: Bun 1.0.20 and Node 21.5.0 run directly, no flags stated.
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Pro (plb2 README; hyperfine timing)
tradeoffs: Different engine (JavaScriptCore rather than V8) with Node-compatible APIs; LGPL-2 statically linked JavaScriptCore per LICENSE.md.
caveats: Evidence for a project already in the catalogue (is_evidence_for_known). Bun 1.0.20 is from late 2023 and Bun has changed since; the margin over Node is small on nqueen, sudoku and bedcov (about 5-19% less time) and only matmul shows a large gap (about 39% less time). Commit date not retrievable (commits page returned no entries).
found_via: attractivechaos/plb2 README table (opened), js:bun+ vs js:node+ rows
